scope: All 38 chat records, all 36 agent message bodies, corresponding call records, first-turn system/input prompts and scratchpad protocol adoption. No API requests or raw-log edits.
central_finding: They independently proposed and converged on glyph-encoded ASCII English. A shared three-glyph transport code emerged: 𗄌=0, 𗅋=1, 𗈰=byte separator; each 8-bit group is an ASCII character. This is an emergent communication convention built on pre-existing English/ASCII, not evidence of a new semantic language.

other_messages: One unnegotiated two-glyph feature/value index proposal

decoding_error.cause_observed: Agents2 and6 independently misread agent5's valid contiguous blue message as yellow. Neither sends yellow in public chat. No transmitter corruption or direct misinformation propagation is visible.

agent6_corrects.basis_claimed: Re-decoded original agent5 blue bytes after score round1 identified clothing_colour as the sole imperfect feature

decoding_error.context_window: All38 chat records fit within50-message window, so messages were never evicted. Wrong private interpretation persisted despite correctly encoded original and clarification remaining visible.

interpretation_limits: There is real decentralized selection/adoption of glyph roles and interoperability across encodings.
No system prompt provides ASCII, Morse, Unicode sorting or glyph meanings; those conventions came from model prior knowledge.
Unicode sorting gives a canonical order despite shuffled presentation; glyph identity itself remains common across agents.
A reserved glyph provides separation without literal spaces. Fixed-width ASCII also works without any delimiter, as agent5 demonstrated.
Shared code encodes English labels/values rather than learning compact feature-specific glyph meanings. The only compact two-glyph semantic proposal was abandoned.
Question mark and equals/underscore punctuation are encoded as ASCII; there is no newly demonstrated grammatical system.
Scratchpad and interview statements are model-written explanations. The literal payload decoder is stronger evidence for exact message contents.
A single episode establishes successful protocol use in this setting, not across-run generalization or novelty of language.
